items.bodyEn: Mariko was among the smallest post towns; the 1843 survey counted about two dozen inns and under a thousand residents. Its fame was tororo-jiru, grated mountain yam in miso broth poured over barley rice, sold at teahouses. Hiroshige's 'Mariko: Famous Teahouse' shows two guests eating it under a blossoming plum while the hostess, baby on her back, serves.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, 'Mariko: Famous Teahouse' (Hōeidō); 東海道宿村大概帳 (1843)

items.bodyEn: Mariko's soup entered literature. In 1691 Bashō saw a disciple off toward Edo with the verse ume wakana Mariko no shuku no tororo-jiru: plum blossom, young greens, Mariko's tororo soup, three tastes of early spring. A century later Ikku's comic road novel Hizakurige sent its heroes to a Mariko teahouse, where a quarrelling couple spill the soup.

items.kana: うめわかなまりこのしゅくのとろろじる

items.bodyEn: Both mark a purpose, but they pick different verbs. ために follows an action you control, with the same doer in both halves: にほんにいくためにちょきんする, 'I'm saving to go to Japan'. ように follows what you cannot simply decide, potentials, negatives and non-volitional verbs: よめるように, 'so that I can read'; わすれないように, 'so as not to forget'; まにあうように, 'so as to be in time'.
items.ja: {忘|わす}れないように、メモしておく。
items.kana: わすれないように、メモしておく。

items.bodyEn: Senri no michi mo ippo kara: even a road of a thousand ri starts with a single step, from the Daodejing. A ri was about 3.9 kilometres, and the Tōkaidō from Nihonbashi to Kyoto ran roughly 126 ri, about 492 kilometres. That makes 〜ようになる, 'come to be able to', the grammar of walking it: nothing at once, everything eventually.
items.ja: {千里|せんり}の{道|みち}も{一歩|いっぽ}から。
items.kana: せんりのみちもいっぽから。
